title: Fractured
author: Tshiamo Ramokgadi
body:
FRACTURED

When what God used in one season becomes the thing that limits you in another.

I need to take you back a bit so you can really understand where my head and heart were.

Before I ever signed my first professional contract, back when I was still playing football at Wits, I broke my collarbone. In an instant, everything I had been building toward felt like it was hanging by a thread. Up until that point, so much of my drive, my vision, and my identity were tied up in the game and what I was trying to achieve.



Looking back now, that broken collarbone was my burning bush moment.

Just like God used a burning bush to stop Moses dead in his tracks in the middle of the wilderness, He used that sudden, agonizing injury to halt me. He used that break to get my attention, to pull me out of my own noise, and to draw me to Himself. That was the season I truly learned how to surrender. I learned how to let God use my brokenness as a testimony.

I never went back to get the surgery done. I stayed with it. I adapted to it. I learned how to live with it, move with it, and play through it. And somehow, God still used me.

In fact, that very broken area became part of my story. It became something tangible I could point to and say, "Look what God has done." It was my living reminder that God doesn't need flawless, unblemished people to accomplish His purpose. He can use broken people. He can use imperfect vessels. He can take the exact thing we thought would disqualify us and turn it into the very place where His power is made clear.



But there is something profound I’ve had to confront in this current season of my life, and I want to share it with you cleanly:



God can use your brokenness without wanting you to remain broken.

Sit with that for a second. Because when that distinction finally hit me, it humbled me to my core.

If you look up the word fractured in the Oxford Dictionary, it’s defined as having a crack, break, or split in a hard material like bone or rock. Figuratively, it describes something that has been split or damaged. 

And every time I read or hear that word, my mind goes straight back to my collarbone.

On the surface, if you saw me walking down the street today, it doesn't look broken. I can move my arm. I can carry my groceries. I can handle my daily work. I live my life just fine.



But if I’m being completely honest with you, there are real limitations:

There are specific ranges of motion I just don't have anymore.

There are certain heavy weights I can’t comfortably lift or carry.

There are subtle ways I’ve trained my body to position that arm because I subconsciously know its limits.

The fracture doesn't shout. It doesn't always announce itself to the room. But it silently dictates my mobility. It changes how I use the arm, how I protect it, and how much weight I let it bear.



And as I’ve been reflecting on this, I realize so many of us are living our everyday spiritual and emotional lives the exact same way.



We walk around fractured. Not necessarily in our bones, but in our hearts.

Maybe for you , it was a harsh word spoken over you when you were younger. Maybe it was a betrayal by someone you trusted with your life. Rejection, abandonment, the sudden loss of someone you loved, or a private pain you’ve never had the courage to speak out loud to a single living soul.



We are all, in some way, living as the sum total of what’s happened to us. But here is the danger we rarely talk about: if we aren't careful, the very thing God used to get our attention in one season can become the limitation that keeps us from going deeper with Him in the next.



Broken, But Surviving

Look around us right now. We are living in a deeply fractured generation—a society full of people who are essentially broken, but surviving.



And man, have we gotten good at surviving. We’ve learned how to function with the pain. We’ve learned how to put on a warm smile. We’ve learned how to show up to work and execute. We’ve learned how to serve in church. We’ve learned how to lead teams. We’ve learned how to hold everything together for everyone else.



But when you sit quietly by yourself at the end of the day, when was the last time you actually asked yourself: "Am I whole?"



Because functioning isn't the same thing as healing. You can learn how to live with a fracture for years. You can master the art of compensating for it and working around it so smoothly that nobody else notices. But eventually, you have to look yourself in the mirror and ask: How long am I going to keep calling survival healing?

There’s a strange irony in my story that I’ve had to wrestle with.

The injury that God used as my burning bush—the very thing that became my primary testimony eventually became my physical limitation. And spiritually, I see so many of us fall into that exact same loop.



There are painful seasons we survived, and because God brought us through them, we built our whole testimony around the scar. The rejection became our key story. The failure became our primary sermon. The heartbreak became the main lesson we share with others to encourage them. We sincerely thank God for bringing us out.



But we get so comfortable telling the story of how we survived the fire that we forget to ask Him: "Father, have I actually let You heal the burn?"



We can unknowingly take pride in surviving things that God is actively inviting us to surrender.

The wound subtly becomes our entire identity. The defensive edge we developed becomes our personality.

The thick wall we built to make sure no one ever hurts us again becomes the very wall that keeps us from receiving real love and intimacy.



Without realizing it... the thing God used to bring us to Him becomes a thorn that keeps us at a distance.



When I was younger, that physical fracture and the emotional baggage tied to it kept me out of certain spaces. But Jesus has been opening my eyes to something crucial lately: It isn't supposed to be the injury that keeps me out of those spaces anymore. It’s supposed to be my deliverance.

Think about it this way: there were places I used to go and things I used to chase simply because I was broken inside. I was running to those environments trying to escape my own thoughts, or trying to fill a hollow space in my chest that I didn't know how to deal with.



Now, Jesus is showing me a better way. I don't avoid those old environments because I'm pretending to be better or stronger than anyone else. I avoid them because Christ is fundamentally changing what my heart hungers for.



The fracture may have kept me away from certain things in a past season out of weakness, but real deliverance teaches me that I don't even want those things in this new season.



Jesus Wants You Whole

If there’s one truth I want to sit on your heart today, it’s this: Christ Jesus genuinely wants you whole.

Not just patched up. Not just functioning. Whole.

He didn't die on the cross merely to forgive our sins on paper while leaving every fractured, hurting piece of our actual daily lives raw and untouched. He came to reconcile us to the Father and to pour complete restoration into every dark corner where sin, suffering, and trauma have taken a toll.



He cares deeply about the parts of your life that nobody else gets to see:



He cares about the health of your mind. He cares about your physical body. He cares about your emotional triggers. He cares about your relationships. He cares about the silent burdens you haven't told a single friend about.

The same Jesus who reached out and touched the man with leprosy is the same Jesus who wants to touch those private places in your soul that you hide from the world. The same Jesus who declared, "I am the bread of life," is the only One who can satisfy that deep craving you’ve been trying to quiet with success, relationships, or distraction.

He is the same Jesus yesterday, today, and forever. Still healing. Still saving. Still restoring. Still transforming.

Wholeness doesn't mean you pretend your past never happened or that you never felt deep pain. Wholeness simply means that your past pain no longer holds authority over who you are today.

A Whole Vessel

Here’s a picture that helped me make sense of all this: A cracked, broken vessel can still hold a bit of water if you balance it just right. But a whole, restored vessel can carry water securely wherever it’s needed without leaking a drop.

That is the invitation God is extending to us right now.

It’s moving past the prayer of: "God, just use me however You can," and stepping into the deeper prayer of: "God, heal me completely so I have the spiritual capacity to carry what You want to pour into me."

Because carrying your purpose requires internal capacity. Sometimes God has to gently heal the survival mechanisms we built in our brokenness before He can safely trust us with the weight of the blessings we've been praying for. Not because He can't use broken people, my own story proves He can but because He loves us way too much to leave us broken.

The Fracture Is Not Your Final Chapter

So as I stand here today, I can look at my life and say: I have fractures, but I am not finished. I carry old scars, but I am filled with real hope. There are still areas where I'm learning to let go and forgive. There are still quiet corners of my heart where I’m asking God for deeper healing.

And I’m not ashamed to admit that to you. Because healing doesn't start when we pretend we’ve got it all together. Healing begins the moment we finally drop our guard, look up at the Father, and get honest:

The same God who met me at Wits, used a broken collarbone like a burning bush, and drew me to Himself is the same God reminding me today that my fracture was never meant to be my permanent identity. What He used to save me in one season was never intended to limit my growth in the next.

And honestly, maybe that’s the greatest testimony we could ever share with the world: Not just that we survived the break, but that Jesus made us whole.

Fractured.

Broken, but surviving.

Wounded, but still standing.

Imperfect, but deeply loved.

And finally surrendered enough to let Jesus heal what I spent years learning to live with.

Because choms, Jesus doesn't just want to use your brokenness. He wants to make you whole.

That's the story
